defects.title: Tracking, click and unsubscribe handlers change state on GET (message log, campaign counters, preferences, consent records) although the manifest records them as read-only.

sourceImplementation.explanation: Unsubscribe GET (the consent-record mutation this title names) now only verifies the signed token and renders a confirmation form; it reads and writes nothing (no withSystemContext, no db call on the GET path). The actual opt-out (preferences, consent record, list subscription) moved to POST, so an email scanner or browser prefetch following the GET link can no longer unsubscribe a recipient. 21+13 regression (route + real in-process SQL) proves no-write GET, forged-token rejection and POST-still-mutates. VERIFIED (follow-up): track/click and track/open's GET handlers do write a clicked/opened timestamp and increment campaign counters on GET, but this is the universal, industry-standard mechanism for email click/open tracking (a mail client's tag and a clicked link are both only ever fetched via GET; there is no POST alternative), and both already bind the action to a destination/campaign-specific signed token (verifyTrackingToken) so a forged or scanner-triggered GET cannot forge an arbitrary redirect or attribute an event to the wrong campaign/recipient - the open-redirect and forgery risks a naive 'GET mutates' framing would flag are independently closed. The manifest's read-only framing was accurate for neither case, but only unsubscribe's mutation carried a real consent-semantics defect (an unintended opt-out); click/open's GET-triggered counters are the correct, intended design.

It is additive, guarded by a snapshot that fails the transaction if any constraint, index, policy, grant or row-security setting changes, and reversible: the rollback removes only the columns and enum types it tagged. A plain Drizzle select through the declaration now succeeds on PG15 and PG16 as the owner and as the runtime role, which holds SELECT on the relation (reachable-stub-shape-2.postgres.test.ts, which fails on the pre-0060 database with the original defect). defects.title: The list, item, tags, compare and search reads run on the system role, which bypasses row-level security, and the only boundary between organizations is a hand-written application predicate; the route comments name this PRIVILEGED_CROSS_TENANT_REVIEW and no kernel decision stands behind it.

sourceImplementation.explanation: The system-role list, search and compare paths now apply a shared source-organization projection. For an anonymized or unclassified clause, cross-organization readers do not receive the source organization id/name; the source owner retains attribution. Search and compare explicitly select the anonymization flag instead of silently omitting it. A unit test covers the disclosure rule and a source contract asserts use in all three routes. The item GET now uses the same source projection and treats an unset anonymization flag as not permission to disclose the original employer; a route regression exercises this legacy-null case. F03-B: the list, search, compare, item and tags reads no longer run on the system role, and the boundary between organizations is no longer a hand-written predicate alone. Cache migration 0048 makes the sharing rule one database rule: public.ue_clause_readable_by (owner, public, explicit grant, same federation, both congress-eligible) with ue_clause_federation_ancestor, ue_clause_congress_eligible and ue_clause_source_name, as pinned-search_path SECURITY DEFINER functions revoked from PUBLIC, and permissive SELECT policies on shared_clause_library and clause_library_tags (a tag follows its parent). The tenant runtime role reads exactly the permitted rows with no application predicate, and sharing-authority.ts and every route ask the same functions, so the route and the policy cannot drift. The native proof found that the earlier system-role reads could not run on the bootstrapped schema: the system role holds no privilege on these tables (requiredSystemPrivileges is empty), so they failed with permission denied; the routes now run as the tenant. Native proof on PostgreSQL 15 and 16 (nine tests): a fixed hierarchy matrix, the real list route as the runtime role, the list equal to the item rule on every pair, tags following the clause, and the functions neither executable by PUBLIC nor a directory. Replaced or adapted tests, disclosed: sharing-authority.test.ts was rewritten (its five tests pinned the removed mocked database helpers) to pin delegation to the database functions, the strict-true admission, the malformed-id fail-closed and the grant-literal sanitising; the route tests now assert the tenant context and that the system role is not used, and their stale mocks and header comments were corrected; clause-library-audit.route.test.ts also repaired a stale DELETE case (the version-history insert added in F06 batch 2 consumed its queued result). B124 CORRECTION of the F03-B account above, which described a design that was refused and is retired. The database functions public.ue_clause_readable_by, ue_clause_federation_ancestor, ue_clause_congress_eligible and ue_clause_source_name (cache 0048) are SECURITY DEFINER functions executable by the tenant runtime role, which the catalog admission contract refuses (a fresh combined bootstrap on PostgreSQL 15 and 16 stopped at its privilege preflight, which the earlier native tests missed because they applied the migrations directly). Cache 0050 drops them and the two policies that called them, with a rollback that restores the 0048 objects. The rule is now stated once, without any function: an organization reads a clause it owns, a clause at the public level, and a private clause that names it in the explicit grant list. That is exactly what the unchanged tenant policies of cache 0011 and 0012 admit, and lib/clause-library/sharing-authority.ts (the item rule canReadSharedClause and the list predicate buildClauseVisibilityCondition) repeats it, so the list, search, compare, item and tags reads still run as the tenant and cannot disagree with the policy. The federation and congress levels are owner-only (fail closed) and the create, update and share routes refuse to set them with a 403, so a clause is never marked as shared with a group that cannot read it. The name of the owning organization of a clause the caller may read, and whose source the projection discloses, is read by id on the system role (sourceNamesFor); the ids come only from rows the tenant policy returned, so it is not a directory of organizations. Re-proven on native PostgreSQL 15 and 16 (twelve tests: the unmodified list route for four organizations against a written-out expectation, the list equal to the item rule on every pair, a stranger reading only what is public, the federation and congress levels readable by the owner alone, the tenant runtime role reading exactly what the rule allows with no application predicate, tags following the clause, no ue_clause_ function left and no SECURITY DEFINER function executable by a business role, the owner name read by id, and the refused share not stored) and by the enforced catalog admission preflight on both versions (ADMITTED, 874 manifest entries). Replaced or adapted tests, disclosed: sharing-authority.test.ts and clause-library-visibility.postgres.test.ts were rewritten for the function-free rule, precedents-item-isolation.pglite.test.ts dropped the 0048 function fixture and strengthened the federation and congress refusal, and the route tests, mocks and header comments that named the removed functions were corrected. The congress_memberships manifest entry no longer lists the clause routes as its readers, because none reads it any more. B125: the onboarding clause suggestions, which read the library through the shared client outside any tenant context, now read as the caller tenant by the same rule, so no read of the clause library depends on the connection role. The sharing change is judged against the level the clause already has (sharingChangeDenial takes the current level, after the ownership check, inside the tenant transaction), so a clause stored at the federation or congress level before they were withdrawn is not locked: its owner can still edit it, and a non-owner who tries gets the not-found answer instead of learning about the sharing rule. The sharing dialog (ClauseSharingControls) no longer offers Federation and Congress as selectable levels (they are shown disabled with the reason), tells the owner of a clause stored at one of them that only their organization sees it, and no longer promises congress-wide access in its privacy notice. Replaced or adapted tests, disclosed: the PATCH and share route tests pinned the denial before the ownership check and now pin the new order (and the owner-success share test uses the public level instead of the withdrawn federation level), a new component test (five tests) covers the dialog, and sharing-authority.test.ts gained the unchanged-level cases. B127: the Full Regression run of f902f8b70 failed one test that B125 had left behind: clause-library-audit.route.test.ts pinned the sharing denial of the share route before the clause is read, and B125 moved it after the ownership check (so a caller who does not own the clause learns nothing from the sharing rule, and the denial can be judged against the level the clause already has). The same repair of the fixture, queueing the owner clause, was made concurrently by another session (43a614ce4, with the tenant-transaction change of the sharing GET in 9b55a6d1c) and is kept as it is; this batch adds the pin that the denial is judged against the clause current level, and records the evidence trail. defects.title: A complaint or suppression event updates the existing communication_preferences row of the one organization and recipient on the message log row, never inserts one and never writes a consent record or touches the distribution-list subscriptions, so a recipient with no preference row stays emailable while the audit record says the suppression was applied, and the same address is not suppressed in any other organization.

sourceImplementation.explanation: A complaint or suppression now creates the preference row when none exists, writes a revoked consent record and the audit entry, and applies once per message in the same transaction. A complaint or provider suppression now ends the recipient's subscriptions to the organization's own distribution lists as well as its preference, and is recorded platform-wide in a governed mechanism: platform 0053 adds email_address_suppressions (SHA-256 of the address only, no plaintext; cache 0043 makes it SYSTEM_ONLY), the webhook writes it in the same transaction as the consent record and the audit entry (only when the event names exactly one recipient; several are not guessed), and the single sending function refuses a suppressed address from any organization and fails closed if the list cannot be read. It is a delivery suppression, not consent, so other organizations' consent records are untouched. A platform administrator lifts one only through an audited route (reason required, row kept); a later complaint clears the lift. Proven on native PostgreSQL 15 and 16 and against a real SQL engine through the webhook. R6 privacy and false-negative review of the address suppression. The stored digest was an unkeyed SHA-256, reversible by hashing candidate addresses; new suppressions are now HMAC-SHA-256 under EMAIL_SUPPRESSION_HASH_KEY when it is set, and lookups and lifts try both the keyed and the plain digest so nothing recorded earlier becomes deliverable. Normalization now covers Unicode form and internationalized domains (punycode, trailing dot); plus-addressing and dots are deliberately not folded. The scheduled-report mailer had a SendGrid path that bypassed the suppression list and, because it swallowed every error with no fall-through, reported success when it sent nothing; it and the unknown-provider branch now fail instead, leaving the one screened sending function.

sourceImplementation.explanation: Closes the regression a subsequent runtime-acceptance review found in the prior batch's delivery (ue_verified_dependency_evidence absent from the canonical storage-authority classification, failing the real catalog privilege preflight on native PostgreSQL 15/16) and extends the verified-dependency architecture beyond decision-engine.ts alone. (1) STORAGE AUTHORITY: registered in db/rls-storage-authority/analytics-ai.ts (TENANT_RLS_REQUIRED, runtime SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE, matching the actual store code), added the Drizzle type-mirror declaration (db/schema/domains/ml/knowledge-transfer-runtime.ts) so the table is canonically declared (matching its ue_cognition_memory sibling) rather than needing an explicit scopeDisposition exception, and regenerated the packaged catalog-authority-contract.json. Verified for real: built a disposable local PostgreSQL 16 AND 15 database via Docker, applied the real migration SQL, ran the actual activateCatalogPrivileges grant-activation function (the same function whose failure produced the reported error) against it - result ACTIVATION_OK on both versions, with the real GRANT confirmed via has_table_privilege to be exactly SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE for union_eyes_runtime and nothing for union_eyes_system, matching the manifest exactly. (2) CONTINUITY-SIMULATOR.TS: gained evidenceBasis:'exploratory_simulation' (type-level marker) and methodologyNote, plus verifiedDependencyContext ({affectedNodesWithVerifiedEvidence, totalAffectedNodes}) computed from the real verified-dependency table for the scenario's actual affected nodes - surfaced through to the frontend (components/knowledge-transfer/propagation-playback/propagation-playback.tsx now renders an explicit 'scenario model, not a confirmed impact' banner with the verified-evidence count). Exploratory simulation is preserved as a labelled scenario model, never gated behind verified evidence (simulation remains a valid discovery tool per the directive), only its evidentiary basis is now explicit and type-checked. (3) EVIDENCE WORKFLOW: a complete authenticated, tenant-scoped application surface now exists - GET/POST at app/api/exit-interviews/verified-dependencies (list, submit) and PATCH at .../[id] (verify/reject/revoke), requiring national_officer+ and a reviewer distinct from the submitter for any review action (enforced by hasMinRole plus the pre-existing DB CHECK), returning 409 on a stale/already-decided/self-reviewed attempt rather than a silent no-op. A reviewer interface (components/knowledge-transfer/verified-dependencies-panel.tsx) is wired into the existing Continuity Planning Workspace as a new tab - no separate application or governance framework was introduced. The continuity decision brief's UI (continuity-planning-workspace.tsx) now also renders confirmedDependencyRisks/confirmedDependencyRiskStatus, which existed in the prior batch's API but were not yet surfaced to any product view. (4) NODE IDENTITY: submitVerifiedDependency and the 'verified' path of reviewVerifiedDependency now call assertNodesCurrentlyExist, which re-resolves the organization's CURRENT propagation map and refuses (with a descriptive error) any node id that does not presently exist there - closing the gap where a label-derived node id could drift out of existence between submission and review without detection. Rejecting or revoking an already-decided/drifted record remains allowed (closing out a stale submission does not require the node to still exist). THIS BATCH (B165) closes the consumer-wiring gap the prior batch (B164) left open: built ONE shared, typed graph-evidence contract (lib/knowledge-transfer/propagation/graph-evidence-service.ts - loadGraphEvidence, hasVerifiedRelationship, hasAnyVerifiedEvidence, evidenceBasisForNode/Pair, confirmedForNode, GRAPH_EVIDENCE_METHODOLOGY_NOTE) plus a bounded canonical node-identity module (graph-identity.ts - canonicalNodeIdentityKey, resolveCurrentNodeId) that makes verified-evidence lookups tolerant of case/spacing/punctuation/diacritic drift in a label-derived node id without ever conflating two genuinely different nodes. Wired all 8 named consumers through this ONE contract in a single coordinated pass: cascade-analyzer.ts and graph-reasoner.ts now tag each governance node/cascade-risk/finding with a per-item evidenceBasis (verified|exploratory); resilience-calculator.ts, continuity-forecaster.ts, mitigation-comparator.ts and strategy-modeler.ts (all whole-graph aggregate consumers) now report a verifiedEvidenceCoverage:{nodesWithVerifiedEvidence,totalNodes} aggregate signal instead of a per-item tag, which is the semantically correct granularity for an index/forecast/roadmap/comparison; copilot-engine.ts now discloses verified-vs-exploratory counts both INSIDE the AI system prompt (so the model itself is told which counts are confirmed) and in the structured CopilotQueryResult; kernel-bridge-foundational.ts was read in full and requires no change - it is a pure (orgId)=>Promise<T> passthrough wrapper, so every evidence field the 7 underlying engines (resilience-roadmap, cascade-risks, continuity-forecast, dependency-propagation, etc.) now return flows through it unmodified, confirmed via its own 35-test suite passing unchanged. verified-dependency-store.ts's assertNodesCurrentlyExist was switched from exact-string to resolveCurrentNodeId canonical-identity-tolerant matching, so a verified submission/re-verification is no longer wrongly rejected (or wrongly accepted against the wrong node) by label reformatting alone. Frontend: governance-impact-explorer.tsx, continuity-planning-workspace.tsx and continuity-simulation-workspace.tsx (the 3 workspaces that render these 4 consumers' output) now render the evidenceBasis/verifiedEvidenceCoverage/methodologyNote fields as explicit badges/disclosure lines rather than silently dropping them in their view-model transforms (workspace-data.ts's toGovernanceImpact/toMitigationView updated to carry the new fields through instead of stripping them). Two new direct unit-test files (graph-identity.test.ts: 13 tests: canonicalization, collision-resistance, non-string defensive bound, resolveCurrentNodeId exact/tolerant/absent/empty cases; graph-evidence-service.test.ts: 14 tests: loadGraphEvidence composition, hasVerifiedRelationship direction-and-tolerance, hasAnyVerifiedEvidence, evidenceBasisForNode/Pair, confirmedForNode's 3 states including a 20-node exhaustive non-substitution proof) prove the shared contract's own logic directly rather than relying solely on indirect coverage through 8 separate consumer test files. ROUND 5 (B166) directly answers four source-engineering requirements raised in acceptance review, none of which the B165 batch actually built despite naming them as known gaps: (A) EVIDENCE LIFECYCLE INTEGRITY - ue_verified_dependency_evidence gained source_fingerprint (a deterministic sha256 of each node's semantic identity, excluding volatile fields like frequency), computed at submission and recomputed at every re-review; loadGraphEvidence now recomputes each nominally-verified record's current fingerprint at READ TIME and splits results into verifiedRelationships (fingerprint still matches, node still resolvable, and - if the evidence is a document reference - the document still resolves) versus a new staleVerifiedRelationships array carrying typed staleReasons (node_no_longer_current, source_fingerprint_mismatch, evidence_reference_no_longer_resolves); a null stored fingerprint (legacy row) is treated as a mismatch, i.e. fails closed rather than silently passing. lookupVerifiedDependency returns a new requires_reverification reason instead of treating a stale record as confirmed. Audit history (status, reviewedBy, reviewedAt) is never deleted or overwritten by this check - only the READ-TIME interpretation changes. (B) DURABLE GRAPH IDENTITY - a new ue_graph_node_alias table (RLS-closed via ue_create_direct_org_rls_policy, same pattern as every other direct-org table) stores an explicit, human-reviewed aliasLabel -> canonicalConceptLabel mapping with superseding (never deleting) history; graph-identity.ts's new resolveConceptLabel checks cosmetic-drift-tolerant matching first (unchanged from B165) and then, only on failure, checks whether the id matches a recorded alias, resolving through the alias to its canonical concept - it never fuzzy-guesses across unconnected canonical keys. A new API route (app/api/exit-interviews/node-aliases) lets a national_officer+ record and list these mappings; every currentness check in verified-dependency-store.ts and graph-evidence-service.ts now resolves through this alias-aware path instead of the plain cosmetic-only canonicalNodeIdentityKey. (C) CONSUMER ENFORCEMENT (OUTPUT, NOT LABEL) - cascade-analyzer.ts's GovernanceCascadeAnalysis now returns confirmedCascadeRisks and exploratoryCascadeHypotheses as two separate, pre-filtered arrays (not just an evidenceBasis tag a caller could ignore); graph-reasoner.ts's QueryResult gained the equivalent confirmedFindings pre-filtered subset; the governance-impact-explorer.tsx frontend renders the confirmed set in its own red 'Confirmed Critical Governance Continuity Gaps' section, visually separated from an explicitly-labelled grey 'Exploratory ... (not yet verified)' section, and the summary tile count now reflects the confirmed subset, not the raw exploratory count. mitigation-comparator.ts's residualRisks (a discrete, per-node 'X remains single-source' claim, the same risk-adjacent pattern as cascade-analyzer) now names each entry's evidence basis inline via evidenceBasisForNode rather than presenting an unqualified sentence. The remaining aggregate-style consumers (resilience-calculator.ts, continuity-forecaster.ts, strategy-modeler.ts, copilot-engine.ts) were reviewed against the same test (does this consumer make a discrete, per-item claim that reads as an established fact, independent of its own aggregate verifiedEvidenceCoverage field) and judged NOT to need the same restructuring: their outputs are composite scores/trend labels/strategy recommendations, not discrete per-node risk assertions, and already carry verifiedEvidenceCoverage plus pre-existing methodology disclaimers from earlier batches (B77/B140/B157) - this judgment call is disclosed here rather than silently assumed, and is a legitimate follow-on item if a future review finds a specific discrete claim inside any of those four this round did not surface. (D) EVIDENCE-REFERENCE VERIFICATION - submitVerifiedDependency's evidenceReference free-text field is now paired with a required evidenceReferenceType ('document' | 'external_citation') and an optional evidenceDocumentId; a document-typed submission is validated at submit time via evidence-document-reference.ts's resolveEvidenceDocumentForSubmission, which loads the real document row (same organization, status active) and runs it through the EXISTING authorizeDocumentsForActor authority check (explicit grants, case access, privacy-label policy) using the submitter as actor - a reviewer no longer has to trust an unverified string plus a manual click-through. documentCurrentlyResolves (a system-level existence+active-status check, no per-actor authorization, to avoid leaking one actor's authorization signal to a different reader) is called at READ TIME by staleReasonsFor, so a document that is later archived or deleted causes the relationship to move into staleVerifiedRelationships on the very next read, not just at the next manual re-review. FAMILY 1 FINAL EVIDENCE-CONTRACT CORRECTION (B167, PR #1137): (1) DIRECTION - the undirected hasVerifiedRelationship is removed; every claim is a directed edge (dependent, dependsOn) matched on RESOLVED current node ids, so A->B never confirms B->A, in the envelope, the single-pair lookup and every consumer. (2) CLAIM-LEVEL CONFIRMATION - node-participation confirmation (hasAnyVerifiedEvidence, evidenceBasisForNode, confirmedForNode, verifiedNodeKeys) is removed; assessDependencyClaim confirms a single edge or a chain only when every directed edge is current-verified, returning the backing records and the weakest evidence tier, otherwise a hypothesis with a reason. Cascade analysis confirms only impacted areas reached by a fully verified impact chain (verifiedImpactChains) and keeps severity exploratory; graph-reasoner node findings are always exploratory and path findings are confirmed per chain; the decision engine reports only current verified dependencies with their tier (and a requires_reverification status); the simulator discloses verified impact chains; resilience/forecast/mitigation/strategy/copilot aggregates report directed edge coverage (verifiedEdgeCoverage), never participating nodes. (3) IDENTITY - identity key version 2 (underscores, case, NFC, whitespace only; v1 stripped accents/punctuation and collided C++/C, Cote/Cote-accented, Re-hire/Rehire); resolveNodeReference reports a collision of current nodes or aliases as ambiguous (never first-match-wins); submissions and verifications store the RESOLVED node ids; aliases supersede by identity key, refuse no-op and alias-to-alias targets, and serialize per organization; any change of which node a reference names, or of its classification, requires re-verification. (4) ONE CURRENTNESS EVALUATOR - graph-evidence-evaluator.ts evaluateRecordCurrentness is the only definition of current, used by loadGraphEvidence, lookupVerifiedDependency, the reviewer listing and re-verification; it checks status, resolution, the versioned fingerprint (a v1 fingerprint is trusted only while its legacy key names exactly one current node), document content integrity and external attestation; reverifyVerifiedDependency is the explicit, distinct-reviewer, optimistic-concurrency path that brings a stale record current. (5) EXTERNAL EVIDENCE TIERS - platform 0087 binds document evidence to its exact content (version:n:content_hash or sha256) captured at submission and verification, adds external_attestation/attested_by/attested_at (all-or-none, external only, attester distinct from submitter, DB CHECK) and identity_key_version; tiers are system_resolved_document, human_attested_external, and unverified_external_citation (never confirms). Drizzle now declares every 0085-0087 CHECK and the unique active-alias index so the V2 bootstrap plan carries them. (6) JOURNEYS - reviewer panel shows currentness, tier and stale reasons, takes the written attestation, offers re-verify; a node-alias management panel shows each alias's current resolution; routes map unresolvable/ambiguous nodes to 409 and correctable input to 400. Both panels previously read json.data as the list although withApi wraps the handler result ({success, data: {data}}), so the reviewer list never rendered; they now use envelopeRows/readApiError. (7) REGRESSION FROM THE EARLIER FAMILY 1 BATCH - 4cc32f6bc renamed the expertise-map field riskLevel to coverageConcentrationLevel, but organizational-memory-explorer.tsx still sorted and coloured topics by riskLevel (undefined, so every topic rendered and sorted as the lowest level) and continuity-heatmap.tsx still declared it; both now read the returned field, and the response-shape census holds the ceiling at 0.

sourceImplementation.explanation: The claim is bound to the purchaser: the paid-tier webhook records the buyer's e-mail on the assessment, and the claiming account's own e-mail must equal it (case-insensitive), as part of the single conditional write that consumes the token. The claim write also clears the stored capability hash and expiry in the same conditional update that decides the winner, and the claiming browser's cookie is cleared. One gate, authorizeAssessmentAccess, now decides every capability-bearing path (profile, answer, submit, results, report, checkout, resume, and the profile and adaptive-resolution actions the results page uses): an unclaimed assessment keeps pseudonymous capability access, while a claimed one ignores the capability even if a hash survived and admits only the claiming account while it is still a member of the claiming organization, or an administrator of that organization. A plain peer, another organization's administrator and an anonymous holder of the old link are refused (403/401). A claimed assessment cannot mint a new capability cookie and its link cannot be mailed. The ICRA capability ratchet recognizes the new gate. Proven natively on PostgreSQL 15 and 16: six concurrent claimants yield exactly one winner, the capability is gone from the row, and refused claims leave the capability intact.

defects.title: The Shopify webhook receiver answers 200 with received true and error Internal processing error for every thrown failure (so Shopify, which retries only on non-2xx, never redelivers a paid, fulfilled or refund event that failed), and processWebhookIdempotent records the receipt after the handler for ignored results too, so an event ignored because the redemption was not yet found (an orders/fulfilled that arrives before orders/paid is processed) is stored as processed and a redelivery of the same webhook id is skipped as already_processed; the receipt check, the handler and the receipt insert run in separate transactions.

sourceImplementation.explanation: A failure answers 500; an event that cannot be applied yet (a fulfilment or refund for an order not recorded as paid) answers 503 with Retry-After; neither records a receipt, so the redelivery is applied. A receipt is recorded only after the handler, only for a final outcome, and tolerates a concurrent duplicate. The handlers are idempotent on their own state (an order already applied is a success), so the separate receipt transaction cannot lose or double-apply an event. Mutation-proved.

It no longer reads through the shared database client (which, outside a context, reads nothing under row security, so an unrecognised organization or an empty list depended on the connection role): the organization and the clauses are read as the caller tenant, so the candidates are exactly what the row policy shows (an organization own clauses, public clauses and private clauses that name it), repeated by the same visibility predicate the clause routes use, and the organization own clauses are excluded because suggesting a clause back to its owner is no suggestion. The source name no longer comes from the organization relation that resolved to Unknown for every organization but the caller: it is read by id on the system role for the clauses whose source the projection may disclose, and a clause that is anonymized or unclassified is labelled Another organization (source not disclosed) and never named and never described as coming from a parent (an organization that has parents is also offered only non-anonymized clauses of those parents, because being drawn from them would itself say where a clause comes from). defects.title: The signature audit trail rows are plain inserts into signature_audit_trail: the hash_chain column is declared as a future link and AuditTrailService.log never sets it, nothing recomputes the stored file hash after creation or compares it at signing or completion, no row is signed or sealed, and the signer IP address comes from the first value of a client-supplied x-forwarded-for header, the geolocation from the request body and the signature image from any URL the signer posts; the audit route nevertheless returns the rows and, with format=report, a report that the service documents as generated for legal compliance, so a document status, a report and an audit trail are presented as evidence of an e-signature when none of their contents is verified or tamper-evident.

sourceImplementation.explanation: The trail is now tamper-evident. Every event carries a sequence number and a hash over its content and its predecessor's hash (the existing hash_chain column; no migration), written under a per-document advisory lock so concurrent events cannot fork the chain; changing, removing, reordering or forging an event breaks verification at that sequence number (proven on real SQL, including concurrent logging, a changed row, a deleted row, a forged seal and a trail from before chaining). Completion seals the trail: the verified head becomes the last chained event and is repeated in the platform's own hash-chained audit log, and a trail whose chain does not verify is not sealed. The report states what verification found (chained events, unchained earlier events, verified, sealed, where it broke), never a constant. Signing recomputes the stored file hash and refuses a mismatch, and records "verified" or why it could not be checked ("unverified:not_own_storage") on the signing event. The signer address is taken from the trusted end of the proxy chain (UE_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS, default 1) with its provenance recorded and no address recorded when none is trustworthy, where it used to be the first client-supplied value or the string "unknown"; a browser-reported position is no longer stored; the signature must be an inline PNG or JPEG of bounded size, not a link. Proven on native PostgreSQL 15 and 16: the runtime role can read and add trail events but not update, delete or truncate them, and the system role holds no write. R6 re-check of the chain claims: a shortened chain still verified, the seal was checked only against the same table, and a completed document with no seal was described as "not complete". The seal the platform audit log already held is now read back (both stores, head and count only) and the trail is checked against it: events removed from the end, a rewritten and rechained trail, and a removed seal event are each reported, and the document is not called sealed. A read that fails is reported as unavailable (inside a savepoint), never as intact; a missing platform record is reported as "could not be checked", not corroboration; a completed unsealed document says it has no seal. Tail deletion, rewrite-and-rechain, seal removal and the savepoint behaviour are tested on PGlite, and the read-back and the runtime role's inability to update or delete the trail on PG15 and PG16.

defects.title: For a workbook with no claimed_by_user_id, resolveClaimedWorkbookAuthority returns the preclaim authority from the workbook identifier alone, so GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE on /api/workbook/<id>/memory-holders run in the system context for any caller who presents that identifier, with no session, with no guardPublicIntake or other rate limit (the route files import none), and auditClaimedWorkbookWrite returns at once for a preclaim authority so the create, update and delete are not recorded; the same identifier is returned by the public start route and placed in the checkout redirect addresses, and each write may carry a display name and notes of up to 4,000 characters.

sourceImplementation.explanation: The collection reads and writes run through the public-intake guard (rate limit; body cap on writes). Claimed-workbook writes were already audited. A miss on a claimed workbook (a PATCH or DELETE that matched no holder) is recorded as an attempt (update_not_found, delete_not_found) rather than leaving no trace. The collection and item routes are behind the public-intake guard and the per-workbook cap of 200 holders was already in place. Two tests that pinned "a miss records nothing" were replaced (disclosed). Pseudonymous audit authority: reads, creates, updates and deletes of the people an unclaimed workbook names are now recorded in a deliberately scoped, platform-level, append-only store (platform 0054, cache 0044, SYSTEM_ONLY, system role SELECT and INSERT only, UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE refused by trigger). No organization, actor or consent is invented: the subject is a keyed HMAC of the bearer identifier (the identifier itself is never written; without PUBLIC_INTAKE_AUDIT_KEY nothing can be recorded and the surface fails closed), details are limited to field names and counts so a typed name, role or note is never evidence, and one subject's events form a hash chain whose fork is also refused by a unique index. A read is recorded before the data is read, in the same transaction, and a mutation commits with its record; if the record cannot be written the read or write does not happen. Claimed workbooks keep their ownership and role controls and now also record reads (previously only writes) under the claiming organization and the acting person. Native PostgreSQL 15 and 16 prove the migrations (twice, rollback and re-apply), the role boundary, concurrent writers on separate connections not forking a chain, and that the verifier catches a rewritten event and a removed middle event. The last open part of the defect, the identifier as the credential, is closed. An unclaimed workbook now has a separate bearer capability (hash and expiry, migration 0056; the token is returned once at start with an HttpOnly cookie) and every memory-holder read, write, change and removal, and the server-rendered page, require it; a missing, wrong, expired or never-issued capability answers as a workbook that is not there. The claim removes it in the claim's own statement and clears the cookie. The memory-holder page, which read the people and their notes directly with no authority and no record, now runs through the same boundary and records the read first. The /workbook/start page inserted workbooks on a plain GET with no limit, challenge or capability; it now renders a control that calls the guarded start API. Natively the system role under which the unclaimed path runs held no INSERT on workbooks and no privilege on workbook_modules or workbook_memory_holders, so none of it could operate; the manifest now declares what the path needs and a native test on PG15 and PG16 proves start, read, add, change and remove under the system role, the consistent capability pair, the claim clearing it, and a tenant role seeing nothing. Replaced tests, disclosed: the access-control "allows an unclaimed workbook via the bearer id alone" test (now capability-gated, with refusal cases), the memory-holder route tests' preclaim fixtures (the capability predicate is a seam there, proven for real in access-control and capability tests), and the two route tests that pinned the boundary arguments.

The unapproved policy requires delivery_verified for a display name or private note, and a looser requirement counts only with an approver. A name or note can therefore not be newly written until a verifier exists (clearing one is always allowed), the refusal is recorded without the value, and what already exists is withheld from every reader except the claimant (peers and the capability bearer get null and a withheld flag; the page, which read the names directly with no projection at all, now applies the same projection on the server so the value is not in the payload). The role, responsibility and every other field still work, so the workbook serves people who are not named, and the client disables the name and note fields unless they are writable. Nothing is sent and no one is marked notified without evidence. defects.title: ue_authority_reviews holds the complainant, the adverse parties and the privileged classification of every review of an organization, and the only row-level-security policy on it is the organization-only policy ue_create_direct_org_rls_policy (migration 0020) while the storage-authority manifest requires SELECT on the table for the tenant runtime role; the rules that hide a review from its adverse party, show an overseer only the reviews a live monitor mandate names, and omit respondent identifiers are SQL predicates and kernel calls inside lib/authority/store/review-intake.ts, so any other query that runs in an organization context can read every review of the organization and the database enforces none of those rules.

sourceImplementation.explanation: F03-A: cache 0047 adds a restrictive SELECT policy for the runtime role to ue_authority_reviews, so the database itself now enforces the visibility rules that lived only in review-intake.ts. A principal named as an adverse party sees nothing of the review, even holding a live mandate that names it; every other principal sees only the reviews they opened or filed, or that a live, accepted, unrecused governance_review mandate names (the kernel's own liveness test: status active, not revoked, inside its window, accepted when acceptance is required). A review the principal cannot see is not found, so the kernel denies it as RESOURCE_FACTS_MISSING, identical to a review that does not exist: a denial no longer confirms that someone is a respondent. The event history was the same data by another route: ue_authority_events keeps a full snapshot (complainant, adverse parties, classification) and the acting principal of every review write, and every member could read it, so a second restrictive policy makes an event of a review exactly as visible as the review (its subquery is itself subject to the first policy). registerReview refuses a review that names its own opener or complainant as adverse (SELF_ADVERSE) and the database independently refuses that INSERT ... RETURNING. Grants, FORCE RLS, the append-only guards and the actor-binding triggers are unchanged, and a re-run of 0020 cannot undo the policy because it is a separate restrictive policy. Proof: 21 PGlite and 21 native tests on PG15 and PG16 as the real runtime role, including the control in which, without the policies, a member who is neither party nor overseer reads every review and every snapshot. Tests adapted and disclosed: authority-kernel-resources.pglite (the adverse reviewer's denial is now RESOURCE_FACTS_MISSING and never ADVERSE_PARTY; the pure-kernel rule stays pinned in kernel-governance.test.ts), authority-kernel-storage.pglite (the review register and the event history carry one restrictive policy each, so six, and no other authority relation has one), and the harness newUuid (a random per-process base, so native suites re-run in one database instead of colliding on append-only ids).
